extracted.intended_audience: graduate students (and advanced undergraduates) studying algebraic geometry; readers of Vakil's Foundations of Algebraic Geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, fundamental properties, and exercises concerning normalization, reduction, and the notions of diagonal, quasiseparatedness, separatedness, and varieties for schemes; includes key theorems (finiteness of integral closure, Cancellation Theorem) and canonical examples. Intended as textbook material for learning and exercising these concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalization — informal purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Normalization is a means of turning a reduced scheme into a normal scheme; in dimension one (reasonable Noetherian circumstances) normalization “resolves” singularities of curves but not necessarily in higher dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reducedness is not strictly necessary for the construction (normalization factors through the reduction). Think of normalization as producing a normal scheme X' together with a morphism X' → X which often 'separates branches' (examples: nodal cubic, cusp, tacnode). See Exercises 10.7.E–10.7.G for examples and Figure 10.5 for picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalization — universal property and uniqueness
rubrics_metrics.description: A normalization of a reduced scheme X is a morphism ν : X' → X from a normal scheme X' such that ν induces a bijection of irreducible components (and in reasonable cases gives a birational morphism on each irreducible component) and satisfies the obvious universal property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the universal property, the normalization (if it exists) is unique up to unique isomorphism. See (10.7.0.1) and surrounding discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalization for irreducible affine schemes (concrete construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X = Spec A with A an integral domain, then the normalization is Spec Ā where Ā is the integral closure of A in its fraction field K(A); ν : Spec Ā → Spec A satisfies the universal property of normalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 10.7.A: verify the universal property. En route, show global sections of an irreducible normal scheme are integrally closed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of normalizations of integral schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Normalizations of integral schemes exist in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 10.7.B: important existence result (hint: ideas from existence of fibered products, §10.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalizations are integral and surjective
rubrics_metrics.description: The normalization morphism is integral and surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 10.7.C: use the Lying Over theorem for surjectivity (cf. 8.2.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalization in function field extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an integral scheme X and an algebraic field extension L of the function field K(X), the normalization of X in L is a dominant morphism ν : X' → X with X' normal and function field L, universal for this property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 10.7.I: show existence when L/K is finite; see also arithmetic and geometric examples (10.7.J and following).

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalization of reduced schemes with multiple components
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend the notion of normalization to reduced schemes with possibly more than one component by defining the universal property and requiring that every affine open subset has finitely many irreducible components (this includes all locally Noetherian schemes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 10.7.D discusses the definition and existence (see Stacks tag 035Q for a reference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalizations often resolve curve singularities (dimension one)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the provided curve examples (nodal cubic, cusp y^2 = x^3, tacnode y^2 = x^4), normalization separates branches and removes singularities in dimension one under reasonable hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises 10.7.E–10.7.G: hints include guessing coordinates (e.g., t = y/x for the nodal cubic) and checking integral closure; note that normalization will not necessarily resolve singularities in higher dimensions (example: the cone z^2 = x^2 + y^2 is normal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rings of integers as normalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: For X = Spec Z and a finite extension K/Q, the integral closure of Z in K is the ring of integers OK, which is the normalization of Spec Z in the extension Q → K.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark 10.7.1: OK is a normal integral domain, Noetherian (Theorem 10.7.3(a)), and of dimension 1; these rings are Dedekind domains (see §13.5.16). Exercise 10.7.J asks to find the integral closure of Z in Q(i).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finiteness of integral closure (Theorem 10.7.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a Noetherian integral domain, K = K(A), and L/K is a finite field extension with B the integral closure of A in L, then: (a) If A is integrally closed and L/K is separable, B is a finitely generated A-module. (b) If A is a finitely generated k-algebra, then B is a finitely generated A-module (E. Noether).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sketch of proof is given (10.7.5) using Galois reduction and linear algebra tricks for (a) and Noether Normalization for (b). See Eisenbud references for full proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning: integral closure need not preserve Noetherian property
rubrics_metrics.description: Part (b) does not hold for Noetherian A in general — the integral closure of a Noetherian ring need not be Noetherian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark 10.7.4: consult Eisenbud for discussion and an example; this indicates Theorem 10.7.3 is nontrivial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finiteness of normalization of finite type k-schemes (Exercise 10.7.M)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is an integral finite type k-scheme, then its normalization ν : X' → X is a finite morphism. Variants: locally Noetherian integral schemes and finite separable field extensions give finite normalization morphisms; normalization in finite extensions of function fields is finite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 10.7.M works out finiteness consequences and implications for varieties (once 'variety' is defined).

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalization morphism is birational and isomorphism on dense open (Exercises 10.7.N,O,P)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is an integral finite type k-scheme, then the normalization morphism is birational (10.7.N) and is an isomorphism on an open dense subset of X (10.7.O). Moreover, a finite birational morphism from an integral finite type k-scheme to a normal integral finite type k-scheme is an isomorphism (10.7.P).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hints reference prior propositions (e.g., Proposition 7.5.7) and exercises; these establish the birational/natural properties of normalization in finite type settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of schemes — definition and construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The reduction X_red of a scheme X is a reduced scheme with morphism ρ : X_red → X such that any morphism from a reduced scheme W → X factors uniquely through ρ; equivalently (affine case) ρ : Spec A/N(A) → Spec A satisfies the universal property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 10.7.6 revisits reduction and Exercise 10.7.Q(a–c) asks to prove existence and compatibility with earlier definitions (9.4.10). The 'red' construction gives a functor from schemes to reduced schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation for separatedness — analogy to Hausdorff
rubrics_metrics.description: Separatedness is the scheme-theoretic analog of the Hausdorff condition for manifolds; the diagonal morphism plays the central role in the definition and consequences of separatedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 11.1 gives geometric motivation: separatedness excludes pathological objects like the line with doubled origin; see Exercise 11.3.B for topological motivation (a topological space is Hausdorff iff its diagonal is closed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagonal morphism — basic properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Given π : X → Y, the diagonal δ_π : X → X ×_Y X is a morphism; if X and Y are affine then δ_π is a closed embedding; in general δ_π is a locally closed embedding and its image (the diagonal ∆) is a locally closed subscheme of X ×_Y X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 11.3.1(a–b) gives the affine calculation and the covering-by-affine-opens argument to see δ_π is locally closed in general. The diagonal is central to definitions of quasisep./sep.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cancellation Theorem for a property P of morphisms (Theorem 11.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let P be a class of morphisms preserved by base change and composition. In a commuting diagram X --π→ Y and Z --ρ→ Y with ρ ∈ P_δ (i.e., δ_ρ ∈ P) and τ ∈ P, then π ∈ P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rather useful abstract theorem is proven via the Diagonal-Base-Change diagram; many concrete consequences arise by plugging in various P (see Exercise 11.3.E and subsequent discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: P_δ is reasonable if P is reasonable (Theorem 11.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If P is a 'reasonable' class of morphisms (preserved by composition, base change, and local on target), then the class P_δ of morphisms whose diagonal lies in P is also 'reasonable'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises 11.2.B–D guide through verifying the axioms of 'reasonableness' for P_δ (preserved by composition, base change, local on the target).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasiseparated morphism (redefinition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is quasiseparated if the diagonal δ_π : X → X ×_Y X is quasicompact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 11.2.G: this agrees with earlier definitions — equivalent condition: for any affine open Spec A ⊂ Y and two affine opens U,V ⊂ X mapping to Spec A, the intersection U ∩ V is a finite union of affine opens. Quasiseparated morphisms form a reasonable class (11.2.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separated morphism — definition and equivalent condition
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is separated if the diagonal morphism δ_π : X → X ×_Y X is a closed embedding. Equivalently, the image ∆ is a closed subset (purely topological condition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 11.3.2 and remarks: separatedness is a property of morphisms and of schemes via their structure map to Spec A. This is the scheme analog of Hausdorff; see Proposition 11.3.1 and Exercise 11.3.B for intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separated morphisms are reasonable (closure properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: The class of separated morphisms is preserved by composition, base change, and the notion is local on the target (i.e., separated morphisms form a 'reasonable' class).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 11.3.3: follows because locally closed embeddings are reasonable and by Theorem 11.2.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affines and finite morphisms are separated
rubrics_metrics.description: Every morphism of affine schemes is separated; hence affine morphisms (and in particular finite morphisms) are separated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 11.3.4: check affine case via ring map surjectivity (Prop. 11.3.1(a)) and use locality on the target.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monomorphisms, locally closed embeddings, and sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Monomorphisms are separated; locally closed embeddings (and open/closed embeddings) are separated. A section σ of a morphism µ is a locally closed embedding; if µ is separated then σ is a closed embedding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises 11.3.C and 11.3.G: apply Cancellation Theorem and properties of graphs/diagonals to deduce these facts; provide counterexamples when separation hypothesis is dropped.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph morphism properties
rubrics_metrics.description: For π : X → Y over Z, the graph morphism γ_π = (id, π) : X → X ×_Z Y is always a locally closed embedding. If Y is separated over Z then γ_π is a closed embedding; if Y is quasiseparated over Z then γ_π is quasicompact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 11.3.6: interpret the image as the graph Γ_π ⊂ X ×_Z Y; useful in many arguments about morphisms and rational maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a variety over a field k
rubrics_metrics.description: A k-variety is a reduced, separated scheme of finite type over k (some sources also require irreducibility or assume k algebraically closed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important Definition 11.3.9: closed and locally closed reduced subschemes of a variety are varieties; morphisms of k-varieties are finite type and separated (Exercise 11.3.J).

rubrics_metrics.name: Products of varieties — conditions and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If k is perfect, the fiber product of k-varieties is a k-variety. (b) If k is algebraically closed, product of irreducible k-varieties is irreducible. (c) If k is algebraically closed, product of connected k-varieties is connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 11.3.11: finite type and separated properties are straightforward via base change and composition; reducedness is handled by reducing to the affine case (Corollary 10.5.22) and separability issues enter when proving irreducibility (Exercise references given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection of affine opens in a separated scheme is affine (Proposition 11.3.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X → Spec A is separated and U, V ⊂ X are affine opens, then U ∩ V is affine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: use Exercise 11.3.M to identify ∆ ∩ (U ×_A V) ≅ U ∩ V; since U ×_A V is affine and ∆ is closed in the product for a separated morphism, the intersection is a closed subscheme of an affine scheme and hence affine. Note: this property does not characterize separatedness (counterexample: line with doubled origin also has this property).

rubrics_metrics.name: Segre/Veronese/linear embeddings give closed diagonal for projective space (example)
rubrics_metrics.description: For P^n_A → Spec A, the diagonal δ: P^n_A → P^n_A ×_A P^n_A is a closed embedding; proofs: (1) direct affine cover calculation, (2) factor δ via Veronese and Segre embeddings which are closed, hence δ sends closed sets to closed sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 11.3.8: two proofs given — coordinate calculation on affine opens and classical geometry factorization using ν_2 (Veronese) and Segre embedding S followed by a linear map L.
